newsitem.title: USA: U.S. unveils new poultry inspection rules.
newsitem.headline: U.S. unveils new poultry inspection rules.

text.p: The U.S. Agriculture Department on Tuesday announced new inspection rules for poultry in a bid to tighten up its policy that no fecal contamination be allowed on bird carcasses.

Feces that spill onto meat when the intestines are removed after slaughter is a major source of contamination by disease-causing bacteria. The biggest food-borne killer, salmonella, lives in the intestinal tract of poultry.

Under current inspection rules, all visible fecal matter must be removed from poultry carcasses by trimming or washing. To underline this "zero-tolerance" policy, the department took "feces" off the list of acceptable poultry defects.

Under the new rule, carcasses contaminated with feces may not enter chilling tanks, the end of the production line. In addition, government inspectors must do spot checks each shift of at least 20 birds after they are washed for the final time. This is in addition to the standard inspection.
"We are reinforcing our policy that contamination is unacceptable," Tom Billy, administrator of the Food and Safety Inspection Service, said in a statement.
The new rule, which was published in the Federal Register, goes into effect on May 5.

"I think putting zero-tolerance for poultry into law is actually a step forward for the department," said Caroline Smith deWaal, food safety director for the Washington-based consumer group, Center for Science in the Public Interest.
The National Broiler Council, an industry group, emphasized the policy was already in place but said its members would work with the department to implement the rule.
"... broiler companies have always had the goal of shipping a product that is free of fecal contamination for the obvious reasons of consumer satisfaction," the group said.

The new poultry regulation is intended to compliment tough meat and poultry inspection rules announced by President Bill Clinton in July, which require slaughter and processing plants to introduce scientific testing over the next three years for sickness-causing bacteria. The first phase of the overhaul took effect last week.

Government inspectors previously relied on sight and smell to certify meat and poultry was safe to eat, a system little changed since Upton Sinclair's expose on the Chicago stockyards, "The Jungle," led to the enactment of the Federal Meat Inspection Act in 1907.
The Agriculture Department estimates five million people become ill and more than 4,000 die each year because of contaminated meat and poultry products.
